transcript: Watching Andrew Scott play every character in Vanya is like watching Picasso at work. This is an astonishing one-man masterclass of a play adapted from Anton Chekhov’s Uncle Vanya. There's so much brilliance to the script and the direction of this piece and the ways they allow Andrew to create an entire world with himself, but for the sake of time, I'll just focus on Andrew's performance. To start, his ability to differentiate the characters is amazing, driven by distinct voices and physicalities and enhanced by smart prop work and implied spatial compartmentalizations. While I think you should be fine without any prior knowledge of the story, my familiarity made me appreciate Andrew’s characterizations even more. And he switches between them with such elegance and seamlessness, while leveraging the one-man theatrical device to add suspense or surprises — there are moments where it's not immediately obvious which character has entered the scene, which feels intentional and adds a new dimension to the flow of information. Another device used a lot here is silence, which Andrew fills with ease — he had us in the palm of his hand and there were numerous moments where you could hear a pin drop. Finally, Andrew's range in this piece isn't just impressive, but it also brings an emotional depth to the story that I hadn't seen before. Throughout, he carries a sharp and funny cynicism while breaking himself wide open to capture the aching despair, regrets, and desires of these characters. He makes their world feel so full and vivid. Vanya is running at the Lucille Lortel through May 11th, though I'm afraid that lottery and cancellation line are the only viable options at this point. With that, another playbill for my collection.
